title: Annular (ring-shaped) rashes: differential
summary: Not every ring is ringworm. Tinea, granuloma annulare, discoid eczema, pityriasis rosea, erythema annulare centrifugum and subacute lupus all form rings. Scale, its position and a skin scraping sort most of them.

glance.think: A ring-shaped or annular patch, especially one that failed antifungal or steroid treatment.
glance.engine: Rings form when inflammation spreads outward and clears centrally; the pattern of scale reflects the process.
glance.backbone: Scrape scaly rings before treating; avoid steroid–antifungal combinations on undiagnosed rashes; biopsy what persists.
glance.never_miss: Tinea incognito, subacute cutaneous lupus (photosensitive, drug-induced), mycosis fungoides and Lyme erythema migrans.

what: *(Module 4 Case 3 teaching frame: solitary annular scaly erythema on chest → later widespread eruption diagnosed as **pityriasis rosea**. Use the initial lesion to practise annular DDx.)*

An **annular (ring-shaped) scaly erythematous patch/plaque** is a common primary-care puzzle. Leading differentials: **tinea corporis**, **annular / plaque psoriasis**, **granuloma annulare** (usually *non*-scaly), **herald patch of pityriasis rosea**, **erythema annulare centrifugum (EAC)**, discoid eczema, and less often subacute cutaneous lupus or erythema migrans.

Reactive figurate erythema; trailing scale; hunt for triggers (infection, drugs, rarely malignancy)

features: **Case 3 arc:** Herald patch misread as isolated annular lesion → antifungal or mild TCS may “fail” as secondary PR eruption appears.

list: History: pets, steroids already used, herald then cascade, joint/nail clues, Lyme geography/tick bite.
**Mycology scrape** before committing to prolonged TCS if tinea plausible (single most useful primary-care test).
Wood’s lamp limited value for most corporis species.
Review in 1 week if solitary lesion — watch for PR secondary rash or tinea expansion.
Biopsy if persistent atypical annular disease (EAC, SCLE, GA confirmation).

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Mycology; PR often follows with widespread oval lesions on cleavage lines
Symmetry, silvery scale, nail/scalp; KOH negative
Expanding after tick bite; Lyme serology/pathway
Coin plaques, very itchy, often legs; not true advancing ring
Photosensitive annular plaques; ANA/Ro; systemic screen

list: **Suspected tinea:** topical terbinafine or imidazole (duration per site/BNF); oral terbinafine if extensive/failed topical — check interactions/LFTs per guidance; treat foot reservoir.
**Suspected PR:** reassure self-limiting (often 6–12 weeks); emollient ± mild–moderate TCS for itch; BAD/PCDS PIL; atypical (palms/soles, very symptomatic) → consider syphilis serology / derm.
**GA:** many localised cases observe; TCS/tacrolimus sometimes tried; extensive → derm.
**EAC:** treat underlying trigger if found; topical steroids symptomatic; derm if persistent.

red_flags: Expanding ring after a tick bite: **erythema migrans**, treat on clinical grounds (NICE NG95).
Photosensitive annular plaques with systemic features or a new drug (PPI, terbinafine, thiazide): think **subacute cutaneous lupus**.
Persistent, fixed, non-healing annular plaques in an older adult: biopsy to exclude cutaneous lymphoma.
pearls: **Never** use potent TCS long-term on an undiagnosed annular plaque — risk of **tinea incognito**.
Explain PR herald → secondary rash so patients do not think treatment “caused” spread.
Recheck feet and nails whenever you diagnose body tinea.
